definitions.definition: "Acquisition", with its grammatical variations and cognate expressions, includes hiring, borrowing, or accepting as a gift.
definitions.plain_english: Acquisition means obtaining or getting possession of an arm or ammunition in any manner. This includes not just buying it, but also hiring it temporarily, borrowing it from someone, or receiving it as a gift. Essentially, any act by which a person comes to hold or take ownership or temporary possession of a firearm or ammunition counts as acquisition under this law.
real_world_examples: A person in Rajasthan purchases a licensed revolver from a registered arms dealer in Jodhpur — this is a straightforward acquisition requiring a valid arms licence.

A farmer in Uttar Pradesh borrows his neighbour's licensed shotgun to protect his crops from wild animals during the harvest season — this borrowing constitutes acquisition and requires the borrower to hold a valid licence.

A relative gifts an old licensed rifle to a family member during a wedding ceremony in Punjab — the recipient is acquiring the arm and must hold a licence and comply with transfer and acquisition formalities.
A security agency in Mumbai hires out licensed firearms to one of its guards for use during duty hours — the act of the guard taking the firearm on hire constitutes acquisition under the Act.
A collector in Chennai accepts a antique pistol as a gift from a foreign visitor — this acceptance as a gift amounts to acquisition and must be covered by the appropriate licence or exemption.

A film production company in Hyderabad borrows prop firearms (capable of being converted to serviceable weapons) from a licensed dealer for a shoot — this borrowing is an acquisition requiring proper licensing.
what_it_covers: Purchasing a firearm or ammunition from a licensed dealer or private party.
Borrowing a firearm from another licence holder, even temporarily.
Accepting a firearm or ammunition as a gift from a family member, friend, or any other person.
Hiring a firearm from a licensed entity such as a security agency or arms dealer.
Receiving ammunition as part of a transaction or arrangement without monetary payment.
what_it_excludes: Merely carrying a firearm in the physical presence of the licence holder or under their written authority (as permitted under Section 3 proviso) — this does not constitute independent acquisition.
Deposit of a firearm with a police station or unit armoury as directed by the Act — such a handover by the depositor is not an acquisition by that person.

Articles designed solely for domestic or agricultural use such as a lathi or ordinary walking stick, which are excluded from the definition of arms entirely and therefore outside the scope of regulated acquisition.
Transfer of a firearm by operation of law (such as by inheritance under prescribed procedures) where the Act provides a separate regime distinct from ordinary acquisition.
The act of a public servant or police officer taking temporary custody of an arm in discharge of official duty — this is not personal acquisition under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes 'acquisition' determines whether a person needs to hold a valid licence under Section 3 of the Act; acquiring any firearm or ammunition without a licence is a punishable offence under the Arms Act, attracting imprisonment and fines. The broad definition ensures that even non-purchase modes of obtaining arms — such as gifts or loans — do not escape the licensing and regulatory framework.

definitions.definition: The term 'aircraft' is not formally defined in the Arms Act, but is used in sections 20 and 26 as a means of conveyance alongside railway, vessel, and vehicle. In context, 'aircraft' refers to any vehicle or craft capable of atmospheric flight, used for transporting persons or goods, upon or within which persons may be employed or working, and which serves as a platform in relation to the carrying, conveying, or concealment of arms or ammunition.
definitions.plain_english: An 'aircraft' in the Arms Act simply means any flying vehicle — such as a plane, helicopter, or similar craft — that can carry people or cargo through the air. The law treats aircraft as a mode of transport where arms and ammunition rules apply. If someone secretly carries illegal weapons on board an aircraft, the aircraft setting becomes legally relevant to the offence and its punishment.
real_world_examples: A passenger on an Air India domestic flight from Mumbai to Delhi is found with an unlicensed pistol hidden in their checked-in baggage, triggering provisions under Section 26 for secret contravention aboard an aircraft.

A cargo handler employed at Indira Gandhi International Airport in New Delhi is found assisting in concealing prohibited ammunition inside a consignment loaded onto a commercial aircraft, making the aircraft a relevant conveyance under Section 20.

A private charter helicopter operating in Jammu & Kashmir is intercepted by security forces after intelligence suggests it is being used to transport arms covertly without a licence, invoking Section 26 relating to aircraft as a means of conveyance.

An airline employee working on a SpiceJet flight route notices a co-passenger transporting what appears to be arms under suspicious circumstances and effects an arrest under Section 20, which empowers persons employed upon an aircraft to do so.

Smugglers attempt to use a small private aircraft in Gujarat to transport prohibited arms across state borders in a manner intended to avoid detection by public servants, attracting the enhanced punishment under Section 26 for secret contraventions via aircraft.
what_it_covers: Commercial passenger aircraft such as those operated by Air India, IndiGo, or SpiceJet used to transport persons who may be carrying arms or ammunition
Private or chartered aircraft and helicopters used to convey arms, whether licenced or unlicenced, in a covert or open manner
Cargo aircraft or freight planes used to transport ammunition or arms consignments, whether or not the crew is aware of the contraband
Any aircraft upon which a person is employed or working, such as airline staff or crew, who may lawfully arrest a person carrying arms under suspicious circumstances under Section 20
what_it_excludes: Ground-based vehicles such as cars, trucks, or trains, which are separately referenced as 'vehicle' and 'railway' in the same sections
Vessels or watercraft, which are explicitly listed separately as 'vessel' in Sections 20 and 26
Unmanned aerial vehicles or drones not used for transporting persons or employed personnel, as the Act's context implies human occupancy or employment aboard the conveyance
Static aircraft on permanent display or in museum settings where no transportation function is being performed
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a contravention of arms licensing provisions (Sections 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, or 12) occurs aboard or via an aircraft determines the applicability of the aggravated secret contravention offence under Section 26, which carries a mandatory minimum imprisonment of six months up to seven years with fine. It also defines the lawful authority of aircraft employees to arrest suspicious persons carrying arms without a warrant under Section 20.

definitions.definition: "Ammunition" means ammunition for any firearm, and includes rockets, bombs, grenades, shells and other missiles; articles designed for torpedo service and submarine mining; other articles containing, or designed or adapted to contain, explosive, fulminating or fissionable material or noxious liquid, gas or other such thing, whether capable of use with firearms or not; charges for firearms and accessories for such charges; fuses and friction tubes; parts of, and machinery for manufacturing, ammunition; and such ingredients of ammunition as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify in this behalf.
definitions.plain_english: Ammunition refers to the cartridges, bullets, shells, and other projectiles used with firearms, but it goes much broader than that. It also covers explosive devices like bombs and grenades, articles designed to carry dangerous chemicals or gases, and even the parts and machinery used to make ammunition. Essentially, anything that is fired from or used to load a gun, or that is designed to explode or release harmful substances, falls under this definition.
real_world_examples: A licensed gun owner in Rajasthan purchases a box of .32 calibre cartridges from a licensed dealer — these cartridges are 'ammunition' and their purchase requires a valid licence under Section 3 of the Arms Act.

A factory in Pune manufactures bullet casings and propellant powder for the Indian Army — both the parts and the machinery used in this process qualify as 'ammunition' under the Act, requiring appropriate authorisation.

A person in Delhi is found in possession of hand grenades without any licence — grenades are explicitly listed as ammunition, and possession without a licence is a punishable offence under Section 25.

A terrorist outfit in Jammu & Kashmir is found storing rocket-propelled grenades (RPGs) and shells — these are covered as ammunition, specifically as 'rockets, bombs, grenades, shells and other missiles', attracting stringent provisions under the Act.

A licensed arms dealer in Mumbai imports fuses and friction tubes from abroad — since these are explicitly listed as ammunition, they require import authorisation under the licensing framework of the Act.

The Central Government issues a gazette notification specifying a newly synthesised chemical compound used as a propellant as an ingredient of ammunition — from that point, possession of that compound without a licence becomes a regulated activity under the Act.
what_it_covers: Cartridges, bullets, and propellant charges designed for use with licensed firearms such as revolvers, rifles, and shotguns.
Explosive devices including rockets, bombs, grenades, and shells, whether or not they are designed for use with a conventional firearm.
Articles designed for torpedo service and submarine mining operations.
Items containing or designed to contain explosive, fulminating, or fissionable material, or noxious liquids and gases, even if not usable with a firearm.
Fuses, friction tubes, and accessories used in the discharge or detonation of ammunition.
Parts and machinery specifically used in the manufacturing of ammunition.
Ingredients of ammunition specifically notified by the Central Government via gazette notification.
what_it_excludes: Ordinary fireworks or pyrotechnic display articles not designed for use as weapons or not notified by the Central Government as ammunition.
Articles designed solely for agricultural or industrial blasting purposes (such as mining explosives) unless separately notified as ammunition by the Central Government under the Act.

Toy cap guns or percussive strips used in toy guns, which are incapable of being converted into serviceable weapons and do not contain fulminating or explosive material of military or offensive grade.
General chemicals or industrial compounds that happen to be flammable or explosive unless specifically notified by the Central Government as ingredients of ammunition.
Weapons themselves (such as the firearm body or barrel) which fall under the separate definition of 'arms' or 'firearms' in Section 2, not 'ammunition'.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an item qualifies as 'ammunition' determines whether a person must hold a licence to acquire, possess, carry, manufacture, sell, or transfer it under Sections 3, 5, 10, and 11 of the Act — unlicensed possession triggers penal liability under Sections 25 and 26, with imprisonment up to seven years. The definition also governs whether an item constitutes 'prohibited ammunition', which attracts the more severe restrictions and penalties applicable to prohibited categories under Sections 7 and 27.

definitions.definition: The appellate authority means such authority as may be prescribed to whom an appeal lies against an order of the licensing authority refusing to grant a licence, varying the conditions of a licence, or suspending or revoking a licence, and whose order confirming, modifying or reversing the order appealed against shall be final.
definitions.plain_english: The appellate authority is the government-designated official or body to whom a person can appeal if a licensing authority refuses, changes, suspends, or revokes their arms licence. This authority hears the appeal, gives the appellant a fair chance to be heard, and passes a final order. Its decision is binding and cannot be challenged further within the same appeals process under this Act.
real_world_examples: A licensed arms dealer in Lucknow has his licence revoked by the District Magistrate. He files a written petition with appeal fee to the State Government's designated appellate authority (e.g., the Commissioner or Home Department) within the prescribed period, challenging the revocation.

A resident of rural Rajasthan is refused a gun licence for self-protection by the licensing authority. He appeals to the prescribed appellate authority, who reviews the refusal and either upholds or overturns the decision, issuing a final order.

A licensed firearms holder in Maharashtra has her licence conditions varied — the permitted calibre of weapon is restricted — and she considers this unjust. She prefers an appeal before the appellate authority within the prescribed limitation period to have the original conditions restored.

An arms manufacturer in Hyderabad whose licence is suspended by the licensing authority pending inquiry approaches the appellate authority seeking a direction to stay the suspension during the pendency of the appeal, as permitted under Section 18.

A tourist residing in Delhi who holds an arms licence finds the licensing authority has refused renewal. He submits a petition in writing with supporting documents before the appellate authority, which has the power to admit the appeal even beyond the limitation period if sufficient cause is shown.
what_it_covers: The authority prescribed by rules to hear appeals against orders of the licensing authority refusing to grant an arms licence.
The authority competent to hear appeals against orders suspending or revoking an arms licence passed by the licensing authority or the authority to whom the licensing authority is subordinate.
The authority empowered to hear appeals against orders varying the conditions of an existing arms licence.
The authority that may conditionally or unconditionally stay the operation of the impugned order pending disposal of the appeal.
The authority whose final order — confirming, modifying, or reversing the original decision — conclusively determines the matter under the Act.
what_it_excludes: The Government itself, since no appeal lies against any order made by or under the direction of the Government, meaning the Government cannot function as an appellate authority under this provision.
The licensing authority whose order is being challenged, as it is the subject of the appeal and not the body empowered to decide it.
Ordinary civil courts or criminal courts, which are not designated as the appellate authority for licence-related disputes under Section 18 of this Act.
Any authority not expressly prescribed under the rules made pursuant to this Act, as the power to hear appeals is conferred only on the prescribed authority.
An authority hearing appeals against orders other than those relating to grant, variation, suspension, or revocation of a licence, such as orders relating to seizure or forfeiture of arms.
definitions.why_it_matters: The designation of the appellate authority determines which body has jurisdiction to grant legal relief to persons aggrieved by licensing decisions under the Arms Act — failure to approach the correct appellate authority within the prescribed period results in the original adverse order becoming final and binding. The finality of the appellate authority's order also limits further statutory review, making it the last avenue of recourse within the Act's own framework.

definitions.definition: The term 'armed forces' as used in the Arms Act refers to the armed forces of the Union, comprising the military, naval, and air forces of India, including members serving in units with designated armouries; where such a member possesses arms or ammunition whose possession has ceased to be lawful, he may deposit the same in a unit armoury instead of a police station or licensed dealer.
definitions.plain_english: The 'armed forces' refers to the official military services of the Indian government — the Army, Navy, and Air Force. Soldiers, sailors, and airmen who belong to these services are treated differently from ordinary citizens under the Arms Act. For example, when they need to deposit firearms they can no longer legally keep, they can hand them over to their unit's armoury rather than a police station.
real_world_examples: An Indian Army soldier whose firearms licence expires while posted in a field area may deposit his personal firearm in his regiment's unit armoury instead of travelling to the nearest police station, as permitted under Section 21(1).

A retired Indian Navy officer who held a personal firearm under a licence that has since been revoked can deposit the weapon in an Indian Naval establishment armoury (which qualifies as a 'unit armoury' under Section 21's Explanation) rather than with a licensed dealer.

An Indian Air Force personnel member who possesses more than two firearms at the commencement of the Arms (Amendment) Act, 2019, and needs to deposit the excess firearm, may place it in his unit armoury rather than at a police station, in accordance with the proviso to Section 3(2).

A serving Indian Army jawan who inherits a firearm and finds that retention would exceed the statutory limit of two firearms may deposit the additional weapon in the unit armoury of his regiment pending legal disposal or transfer.

An officer of the Border Security Force — not being a member of the armed forces of the Union — would not qualify under this exemption and must deposit excess firearms at the nearest police station or a licensed dealer, illustrating who falls outside this definition.

A member of the Indian Navy whose ship-based armoury is designated as a 'unit armoury' under the Explanation to Section 21 deposits his personal licensed firearm there when his licence lapses during a prolonged overseas deployment.
what_it_covers: Members of the Indian Army, including commissioned officers, junior commissioned officers, and other ranks serving in army units with designated armouries.
Members of the Indian Navy, including personnel serving on ships or naval establishments where the ship or establishment armoury qualifies as a 'unit armoury' under the Explanation to Section 21.
Members of the Indian Air Force serving in air force units or establishments that maintain a unit armoury for deposit of arms whose possession has ceased to be lawful.
Situations where a serving member of the armed forces of the Union exceeds the statutory limit of two firearms and needs to deposit the excess in a unit armoury under the proviso to Section 3(2).
what_it_excludes: Paramilitary and central armed police forces such as the CRPF, BSF, CISF, ITBP, and SSB, which are not 'armed forces of the Union' and whose members must deposit firearms at police stations or licensed dealers.
State police officers and state armed constabulary personnel, who are governed by state law enforcement frameworks and are not members of the Union's armed forces.

Civilian defence employees, defence contractors, and non-combatant enrolled personnel who work with or for the armed forces but are not themselves enlisted or commissioned members of the Army, Navy, or Air Force.
Retired or ex-servicemen who have been discharged from the armed forces and no longer hold active membership in a unit, and therefore cannot avail of unit armoury deposit facilities.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a member of the 'armed forces' under Section 21 determines whether he can deposit firearms whose possession has ceased to be lawful in a unit armoury — a significant procedural privilege — rather than being compelled to deposit them at a police station or licensed dealer; failure to avail of the correct deposit mechanism, or unauthorised retention of firearms beyond the prescribed period, can expose the individual to forfeiture of the arms under Section 21(3) and potential prosecution for unlawful possession under the Act.

definitions.definition: "Arms" means articles of any description designed or adapted as weapons for offence or defence, and includes firearms, sharp-edged and other deadly weapons, and parts of, and machinery for manufacturing, arms, but does not include articles designed solely for domestic or agricultural uses such as a lathi or an ordinary walking stick and weapons incapable of being used otherwise than as toys or of being converted into serviceable weapons.
definitions.plain_english: Arms refers to any object made or modified to be used as a weapon for attacking or defending, including guns, swords, knives, and even the parts or machines used to make such weapons. However, everyday household or farming tools like a lathi or walking stick are not considered arms. Similarly, toy weapons that cannot be turned into real working weapons are also excluded from this definition.
real_world_examples: A licensed gun shop owner in Lucknow selling a revolver to a customer holding a valid arms licence — the revolver is 'arms' under the Act and the transaction is governed by licensing provisions.

A blacksmith in rural Rajasthan manufacturing kirpans and swords for sale — the finished blades as well as the machinery and tools used to make them qualify as 'arms', requiring compliance with manufacturing licence requirements.

A Mumbai antique dealer possessing a 19th-century decommissioned cavalry sword as part of a collection — the sword, being a sharp-edged deadly weapon, constitutes 'arms' and requires a valid licence unless specifically exempted.

A toy importer in Delhi bringing in plastic cap-guns that fire only paper caps and cannot be converted into functional firearms — these fall outside the definition of 'arms' as they are incapable of being converted into serviceable weapons.

A factory in Jabalpur (near the Ordnance Factory Board cluster) that produces barrel assemblies and trigger mechanisms for rifles — such parts expressly fall within 'arms' and are subject to all licensing and regulation provisions of the Act.

A farmer in Punjab carrying a kirpan of blade length exceeding the prescribed limit without a licence — the kirpan, as a sharp-edged deadly weapon, constitutes 'arms' and possession without licence is an offence under the Act.

Sharp-edged and other deadly weapons such as swords, daggers, kirpans, and knives designed as weapons.
Parts of arms, such as barrels, triggers, stocks, and firing mechanisms manufactured or sold separately.
Machinery used for manufacturing arms, including lathes and presses specifically adapted for arms production.
Articles designed or adapted as weapons for offence or defence even if not conventionally classified as firearms, such as certain modified tools converted into striking or stabbing weapons.
what_it_excludes: Articles designed solely for domestic or agricultural use, such as an ordinary lathi (bamboo stick) or a walking stick, even if capable of causing injury.
Weapons that are incapable of being used otherwise than as toys, such as plastic cap-guns or rubber-band guns that cannot be converted into serviceable weapons.
Conventional farming implements like sickles, axes, or spades, where the design is primarily agricultural and not adapted for use as a weapon.
Ordinary household cutlery such as kitchen knives not designed or adapted for use as weapons of offence or defence.

definitions.definition: A person is 'authorised' under the Arms Act when they have been granted express permission by the Central Government under Section 7 or are licensed or otherwise permitted under Section 5 of the Act to deal in, possess, carry, or transfer arms or ammunition, as distinguished from a person who merely holds a licence for personal possession. In the context of Section 29, 'authorised' refers specifically to a person who is licensed or authorised under Section 5 to sell, transfer, or otherwise deal in firearms or ammunition.
definitions.plain_english: Being 'authorised' means having official government permission to deal in, sell, or transfer arms or ammunition — this is more than just owning a gun licence for personal use. A licensed arms dealer or someone with special Central Government approval would be 'authorised'. If someone sells a firearm to a person who does not have this authorisation, they can be prosecuted. It is a formal status granted by law, not something a person can claim on their own.
real_world_examples: A registered arms dealer in Agra holds a licence under Section 5 of the Arms Act to sell firearms from his shop — he is 'authorised', so a buyer purchasing from him does not commit an offence under Section 29.

A private citizen in Mumbai who holds a personal arms licence for self-defence is NOT authorised under Section 5 to sell or transfer firearms; if someone knowingly buys a pistol from him, that buyer commits an offence under Section 29.

The Central Government grants special authorisation to a state-owned ordnance factory to manufacture and test prohibited arms under Section 7 — that factory is 'authorised' for those specific activities.

A retired army officer in Delhi tries to sell his licensed revolver to a neighbour without going through a licensed dealer; the neighbour knowing the seller has no dealer authorisation would be committing an offence under Section 29 by purchasing from him.

A licensed arms dealer in Chennai transfers ammunition stock to another licensed dealer in Hyderabad — since both are authorised under Section 5, the transaction is lawful and does not attract liability under Section 29.

A film production company obtains special Central Government authorisation to temporarily possess prohibited arms as props — this authorisation under Section 7 makes their possession lawful for the specified purpose.
what_it_covers: A person holding a valid dealer's licence under Section 5 who is permitted to sell, transfer, or deal in firearms and ammunition commercially.
An entity or individual who has received express special authorisation from the Central Government under Section 7 to manufacture, test, repair, or possess prohibited arms or prohibited ammunition.
A government body, defence establishment, or ordnance factory authorised by the Central Government to deal in or manufacture notified or prohibited arms for official purposes.
A licensed importer or exporter of arms who has been granted specific authorisation under the Act or Arms Rules 2016 to conduct such trade.
A person to whom a specific Section 5 licence has been issued permitting the sale or transfer of arms as part of a regulated commercial activity.
what_it_excludes: An individual who holds only a personal possession licence (e.g., for self-defence) but has no authorisation to sell, transfer, or deal in arms — such a person is licensed but not 'authorised' in the Section 29 sense.
Any person who informally or privately transfers, sells, or lends a firearm without holding a Section 5 dealer's licence or equivalent Central Government authorisation, regardless of their intent.
A person who was previously authorised but whose licence or authorisation has expired, been revoked, or been suspended, as they no longer hold valid authorisation at the time of the transaction.
Security guards or private individuals permitted to carry arms for personal protection — their licence covers possession and carriage, not commercial dealing or transfer.

Members of the armed forces carrying service weapons under military authority — they operate under separate statutory frameworks and are not 'authorised' under Section 5 of the Arms Act for civilian dealing purposes.

definitions.plain_english: Celebratory gunfire refers to the practice of firing a gun into the air during a celebration or festive occasion — such as a wedding, festival, or political event — as a way of expressing joy or marking the occasion. Even though no one is being deliberately targeted, this is treated as a serious offence under the Arms Act. The law recognises that such firing is dangerous and reckless, as bullets can injure or kill people when they come down.
real_world_examples: At a wedding ceremony in rural Punjab, a relative of the groom fires a licensed revolver into the air outside the venue to celebrate the occasion; this constitutes celebratory gunfire and is punishable under Section 25 of the Arms Act.

During a political victory rally in Uttar Pradesh, supporters of a winning candidate fire rifles into the air in a crowded public square; each person who fires is liable for celebratory gunfire under the Act.

At a harvest festival in Haryana, a farmer fires his shotgun into the air as a traditional mark of celebration; despite local custom, this amounts to an offence of celebratory gunfire attracting criminal punishment.

At a New Year's Eve gathering in a residential area of Delhi, a licensed pistol holder fires shots into the air at midnight to mark the occasion; this discharge in a public place constitutes celebratory gunfire under the Arms Act.

During a religious procession in Bihar, members of the procession fire country-made firearms into the air as a customary expression of devotion; such firing is classified as celebratory gunfire and attracts penal consequences regardless of religious intent.
what_it_covers: Firing a licensed or unlicensed firearm into the air at weddings, festivals, or public celebrations.
Discharge of firearms during political rallies, victory processions, or election celebrations in a public place.
Traditional or customary shooting into the air during religious ceremonies, harvest festivals, or community events.
Any reckless discharge of a firearm not directed at a specific target but done as an expression of joy or festivity in a gathering.
what_it_excludes: Firing in lawful self-defence where the discharge is directed at a person posing an imminent threat — this is governed separately under provisions relating to lawful arrest and self-defence.
Controlled discharge by armed forces or police personnel during authorised drills, parades, or ceremonial gun salutes conducted under official sanction.
Testing or proving of firearms by licensed manufacturers or dealers on designated firing ranges under Section 5, which is authorised and regulated activity.
Discharge of firearms by hunters or sportspersons on authorised ranges or in designated areas under a valid licence, which does not constitute celebratory gunfire.

definitions.definition: Every offence under the Arms Act shall be cognizable within the meaning of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (2 of 1974), meaning that a police officer may arrest a person accused of such an offence without a warrant and may investigate the offence without the prior permission of a magistrate.
definitions.plain_english: A 'cognizable' offence is one where the police have the power to arrest a suspect without needing a court-issued arrest warrant. Under the Arms Act, every offence is treated as cognizable, which means the police can immediately act — arrest, search, and investigate — without waiting for a magistrate's approval. This gives law enforcement stronger and faster powers to deal with arms-related crimes.
real_world_examples: A police patrol in Mumbai finds a person carrying an unlicensed pistol; because all Arms Act offences are cognizable, the officer immediately arrests the person on the spot without needing a magistrate's warrant.

During a routine check in Delhi, police discover a trader illegally storing prohibited ammunition in a warehouse; the cognizable nature of the offence allows investigators to raid the premises and make arrests without prior court permission.

A tip-off leads Punjab Police to a suspect transporting a cache of illegal firearms across state lines; officers intercept and arrest the accused on the highway under their cognizable offence powers without obtaining a warrant first.

In a disturbed area in Manipur, security forces identify an individual in possession of notified arms without authorisation; the cognizable classification enables immediate arrest and detention while investigation proceeds.

A licensed dealer in Lucknow is found selling firearms beyond the permitted quantities and without proper documentation; local police arrest him forthwith as the Arms Act offence is cognizable, triggering an immediate FIR and investigation.
what_it_covers: All offences under the Arms Act including unlicensed possession, manufacture, sale, or transfer of firearms and ammunition.
Offences relating to prohibited arms and prohibited ammunition under the Act, making them subject to warrantless arrest.
Illegal transport or import of arms and ammunition, allowing police to arrest offenders on the spot without a warrant.
Possession of imitation firearms in violation of the Act, which is also treated as a cognizable offence.
Contravention of licence conditions by a licensed dealer or any other person, enabling immediate police action.
what_it_excludes: Non-criminal administrative violations or regulatory breaches that do not constitute 'offences' under the Arms Act are not covered as cognizable acts.
Offences under other laws (e.g., the Explosives Act or NDPS Act) committed alongside an arms offence — those are governed by their own procedural classification, not by Section 38.
Civil disputes regarding ownership or succession of licensed arms, which do not constitute criminal offences and therefore fall outside the cognizable offence framework.
Actions by armed forces of the Union operating under special military law, where separate legal regimes may override the standard CrPC cognizability provisions.
Offences by foreign diplomats or persons with diplomatic immunity, who may not be subject to warrantless arrest despite the cognizable classification.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of Arms Act offences as cognizable directly empowers police to arrest without a warrant, register an FIR, and conduct searches and investigations without prior magisterial sanction, significantly strengthening the State's ability to combat illegal arms possession and trafficking. If an offence were non-cognizable, the police would require a magistrate's order before arresting a suspect or investigating, which would critically delay enforcement in time-sensitive arms-related situations.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 33, 'company' means any body corporate, and includes a firm or other association of individuals.
definitions.plain_english: A 'company' under the Arms Act is not just a registered company but any group of people formally working together, including business partnerships and associations. This broad definition ensures that when a group collectively commits an offence under the Arms Act, the law can hold both the organisation and the responsible individuals within it accountable. It is designed to prevent organisations from shielding guilty individuals behind a corporate or group structure.
real_world_examples: A registered private limited company in Mumbai engaged in licensed arms dealing violates storage norms under the Arms Act — both the company and its directors in charge of operations can be prosecuted under Section 33.

A partnership firm in Lucknow holding a licence to manufacture firearm components is found to have illicitly trafficked prohibited arms — all partners of the firm, being members of an 'association of individuals,' are liable alongside the firm.

A trade association in Delhi whose office-bearers collectively and knowingly facilitate illegal acquisition of arms by members can be prosecuted as a 'company' under the Act, with each responsible officer deemed guilty.

A cooperative society in Rajasthan registered under state law, which is also a body corporate, is found to have authorised the unlawful transfer of firearms — the society as well as the secretary and manager who consented to the act face criminal liability.

An informal shooting club in Chandigarh, functioning as an unregistered association of individuals, collectively acquires arms without proper licences — being an 'association of individuals,' the group qualifies as a 'company' under Section 33, and responsible members can be charged.

A Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) in Hyderabad engaged in security services is found to have procured ammunition beyond reasonable quantities without authorisation — the LLP and its designated partners are both liable under this provision.
what_it_covers: Any registered body corporate such as a private limited company, public limited company, or LLP incorporated under Indian law.
A firm, including a registered or unregistered partnership firm constituted under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932.
Any other association of individuals, whether formal or informal, including clubs, societies, or cooperative bodies that collectively act in a manner attracting Arms Act liability.
A cooperative society registered under any state or central law that qualifies as a body corporate.
A foreign company operating in India that commits an offence under the Arms Act through its officers or agents.
what_it_excludes: A sole proprietorship, since it is neither a body corporate nor a firm or association of individuals — liability in such cases attaches solely to the individual proprietor.
A Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) acting in its capacity as a tax or property entity, as it does not constitute a 'body corporate' or a 'firm' in the conventional legal sense under this provision.

Casual or ad hoc groups of individuals with no organisational structure or common purpose who happen to be together at the time of an offence — they are not an 'association of individuals' in the institutional sense intended by the section.
Government bodies or departments acting in their sovereign capacity, as they are typically not treated as 'companies' in the commercial or associational sense under the Arms Act.
Armed forces of the Union, which are separately governed and are not subject to prosecution as a 'company' under this provision.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as a 'company' under Section 33 determines whether its directors, managers, secretaries, partners, or other officers can be personally prosecuted and punished for Arms Act offences committed in the course of the entity's business. Without this definition, organisational entities could escape criminal liability by diffusing individual responsibility, making it critical for determining who faces imprisonment or fines under the Act.

definitions.definition: Contravention, as used in the Arms Act, refers to any act or omission that violates, breaches, or fails to comply with any provision of this Act or the rules made thereunder, including acting without a required licence, exceeding the scope of a licence, or engaging in any prohibited conduct relating to arms or ammunition. It encompasses both active violations and the likelihood of such violations being committed.
definitions.plain_english: A 'contravention' simply means breaking a rule or law — in this case, doing something the Arms Act forbids, or failing to do something the Arms Act requires. For example, carrying a gun without a licence, selling weapons illegally, or transporting arms without permission would all be contraventions. It can mean something that has already happened or something that appears likely to happen.
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai is found carrying a loaded pistol in a public market without holding any firearms licence under Section 3 of the Arms Act — this constitutes a contravention of Section 3.
A licensed arms dealer in Delhi sells prohibited ammunition to a private individual who does not hold the necessary licence under Section 7, thereby committing a contravention of that section.

A truck driver transporting a consignment of rifles across state borders in Uttar Pradesh without the required transport licence under Section 12 is stopped at a checkpoint — this is a contravention of Section 12.

A resident in Jammu who fails to deposit his firearm with the district magistrate as directed under a notification issued under Section 24A continues to possess the weapon — this constitutes a contravention of that notification.

A factory in Madhya Pradesh manufactures revolvers without obtaining the mandatory licence under Section 5, constituting a contravention of that section and triggering search and seizure powers under Section 23.

A person in Chennai shortens the barrel of a legally owned rifle without authorisation, converting it into a more concealable weapon in violation of Section 6, which amounts to a contravention of that section.
what_it_covers: Possessing, acquiring, or carrying any firearm or ammunition without a valid licence as required under Section 3.
Manufacturing, selling, transferring, or repairing arms or ammunition without the requisite licence under Section 5.
Transporting arms or ammunition across state or district boundaries without the required authorisation under Section 12.
Failure to deposit arms or ammunition when directed to do so by the licensing authority under Section 21 or Section 3(2).
Carrying or possessing arms in a notified disturbed area or public place in violation of a notification issued under Sections 24A or 24B.
Bringing into or taking out of India any arms or ammunition without proper authorisation under Sections 10 or 11.
what_it_excludes: Acts that are fully authorised under a valid and subsisting licence issued by the appropriate licensing authority — such conduct does not constitute a contravention.
Possession of arms by armed forces of the Union or other notified government bodies acting within their sanctioned scope, as these are exempt from the Act's licensing requirements.
Actions that merely involve procedural delays or administrative non-compliance where the underlying activity is otherwise lawfully licensed and no substantive prohibition is breached.
Possession of arms by a person who has made a timely application for renewal of an expired licence and continues to hold the arms in good faith pending decision, as permitted under the Act.
Conduct that is not regulated by the Arms Act or the Arms Rules 2016, such as possession of items that fall entirely outside the definition of 'arms' or 'ammunition' under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: The existence of a contravention — or even the likelihood of one — is the legal precondition that empowers magistrates, police officers, and specially authorised officers to stop, search, and seize vessels, vehicles, and conveyances under Section 23; without a contravention, such coercive enforcement powers cannot be lawfully exercised. Additionally, proof of contravention of specific sections directly determines which penal provisions under Section 25 apply, including whether mandatory minimum sentences of imprisonment for two, seven, ten years, or life are triggered.

definitions.definition: Detention, as used in the Arms Act, refers to the lawful holding or restraining of a person by an authority acting under legal sanction, including the act of keeping a person in custody to prevent escape or to preserve public order. In the context of Section 28, it encompasses any lawful detention of a person by a police officer, magistrate, or other competent authority, the resistance to which through use or threatened use of a firearm or imitation firearm constitutes a punishable offence.
definitions.plain_english: Detention means being lawfully held in custody by the police or another authorised authority — for example, being arrested and kept at a police station. If someone uses or threatens to use a firearm to stop themselves or another person from being lawfully held in this way, they commit a serious offence under the Arms Act. It is essentially the legal act of keeping someone in custody, and the law protects this process by making armed resistance to it a crime.
real_world_examples: A suspect in Delhi who is being taken into preventive custody under CrPC provisions pulls out a licensed pistol and threatens the arresting officer to secure his release — this constitutes use of a firearm to resist lawful detention under Section 28.

During a police raid on an illegal arms cache in Mumbai, one of the accused points a country-made pistol at constables attempting to detain him, thereby committing an offence punishable with up to seven years imprisonment under Section 28 of the Arms Act.

A person already detained at a police station in Chennai brandishes an imitation firearm smuggled inside by an accomplice to intimidate the officers and attempt to walk free — this constitutes attempting to use an imitation firearm to prevent lawful detention.

In a Naxal-affected district in Chhattisgarh, a wanted accused fires into the air using a stolen revolver as police attempt to formally detain him after a court-issued warrant, invoking the penal provisions of Section 28.

During a communal tension situation in Uttar Pradesh, a person under preventive detention orders resists transfer between facilities by producing an unloaded country pistol, constituting attempted use of a firearm to prevent lawful detention.
what_it_covers: Formal arrest and custody of a person by a police officer acting under a warrant or under CrPC powers of arrest without warrant.
Preventive detention of a person by a magistrate or executive authority under applicable laws, the armed resistance to which attracts Section 28 liability.
Attempted detention of a person during an ongoing law enforcement operation, where the person uses or threatens to use a firearm or imitation firearm to escape custody.
Detention ordered by any other competent authority recognised under Indian law, such as Customs officers or central government officials, where armed resistance invokes the Arms Act.
what_it_excludes: Unlawful or illegal detention by private individuals or vigilante groups — Section 28 applies only to resistance against lawful detention by authorised authorities.
Detention of arms or ammunition by the Central Government under Section 24, which is a distinct concept referring to seizure and holding of weapons rather than custody of persons.
Mere verbal or physical resistance to arrest without any use, threatened use, or attempted use of a firearm or imitation firearm, which falls outside the scope of Section 28.
Civil or contractual disputes involving holding of property or goods, which are entirely outside the meaning of detention as used in the Arms Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as resistance to 'lawful detention' directly determines if the accused is liable under Section 28, which carries imprisonment up to seven years and a fine — a significantly heavier punishment than general arms offences. If the detention was unlawful, the use of a firearm to resist it may not attract Section 28 liability, fundamentally altering the prosecution's case.

In cities or areas that have a Commissioner of Police, the Commissioner of Police takes on this role instead of the regular district magistrate. In some cases, a Deputy Commissioner of Police designated by the State Government may also act as the district magistrate for arms-related purposes in a specific area.
real_world_examples: In Mumbai, which has a Commissioner of Police, a person applying for a firearm licence under the Arms Act must submit their application to the Commissioner of Police (who acts as the district magistrate), not to the regular District Magistrate.

In a rural district in Uttar Pradesh where no Commissioner of Police has been appointed, the actual District Magistrate (a senior IAS officer) is the authority who grants or refuses arms licences under Section 21 of the Arms Act.

The State Government of Karnataka notifies a Deputy Commissioner of Police of a sub-division of Bengaluru to exercise the powers of the district magistrate for arms licensing purposes in that sub-division, enabling decentralised processing of licence applications.

A licensed arms dealer in Kolkata who intends to transfer firearms to a private buyer informs the Commissioner of Police (acting as district magistrate) in writing, as required, since Kolkata is a Commissionerate area.

definitions.definition: A 'disturbed area' means any area specified by the Central Government by notification in the Official Gazette, where it is satisfied that there is extensive disturbance of public peace and tranquillity, or imminent danger of such disturbance, and that for the prevention of offences involving the use of arms in such area, it is necessary or expedient to impose special restrictions on the possession and carrying of notified arms.
definitions.plain_english: A 'disturbed area' is a specific geographic region that the Central Government officially designates through a gazette notification because it believes there is serious ongoing public unrest or a strong risk of such unrest breaking out there. Once an area is declared 'disturbed,' special rules apply — people must deposit certain weapons, and carrying those weapons in public places becomes prohibited. The government can keep this designation active for up to 90 days at a time, and can extend it repeatedly as long as the unrest continues.
real_world_examples: Certain districts in Manipur or Nagaland experiencing active insurgent activity are declared disturbed areas, requiring civilians holding licensed firearms to deposit them with authorities before the notified period begins.

Parts of Jammu & Kashmir during a period of heightened militant activity are notified as disturbed areas under the Arms Act, prohibiting anyone from carrying rifles or shotguns through markets, roads, or other public places during the notified period.

A border district in Assam experiencing communal violence leading to widespread breakdown of public order is designated a disturbed area, empowering specified officers to search vehicles and premises for concealed notified arms without a warrant.

Urban localities in Chhattisgarh affected by Left-Wing Extremism are declared disturbed areas, triggering mandatory deposit of all notified arms including licensed country-made pistols held by local residents, with possession after the deposit deadline becoming unlawful.

A taluk in Punjab during a period of severe law-and-order breakdown is notified as a disturbed area for 90 days, after which the Central Government extends the notification by a further 90 days upon being satisfied that the disturbance of public peace and tranquillity continues.
what_it_covers: Any area where the Central Government is satisfied there is extensive existing disturbance of public peace and tranquillity, and the limits of which are specifically notified in the Official Gazette.

Any area where the Central Government perceives imminent danger of disturbance of public peace and tranquillity, even if large-scale violence has not yet commenced, so long as a notification specifying its limits is published.
Areas affected by insurgency, communal riots, Left-Wing Extremism, or militant activity where the use of arms in offences is a specific concern prompting the notification.
A notified area remains a 'disturbed area' for the duration of the period specified in the notification, including any extensions granted under Section 24A(2) or Section 24B, up to 90 days at a time.
what_it_excludes: Areas where there is merely localised or minor law-and-order problems that do not rise to the level of 'extensive disturbance of public peace and tranquillity' or imminent danger thereof, as the threshold for notification is substantive satisfaction of the Central Government.

Areas declared disturbed under other statutes (such as under the Armed Forces Special Powers Act, 1958) but not separately notified as disturbed areas under the Arms Act by the Central Government for purposes of Sections 24A and 24B.

Privately held or enclosed premises and localities that fall outside the geographic limits specified in the Central Government notification, even if they are adjacent to or surrounded by the notified disturbed area.

Any area after the expiry of the notified period (including all extensions), as the 'disturbed area' status lapses automatically unless a fresh or extended notification is published in the Official Gazette.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an area qualifies as a 'disturbed area' is the foundational trigger for the special prohibitory and penal regime under Sections 24A and 24B of the Arms Act — without this designation, the mandatory deposit obligation, the prohibition on possessing or carrying notified arms, and the warrantless search and seizure powers conferred on specified officers do not arise. Violations of the restrictions applicable in a disturbed area attract criminal liability under Section 25 of the Arms Act, making the classification directly determinative of guilt or innocence in prosecutions for unlawful possession or carrying of notified arms.

A farmer in Punjab found in possession of an unlicensed country-made pistol (desi katta) is in illegal possession of a firearm and is liable for prosecution under Section 25 of the Arms Act.
A retired army officer retaining his service pistol at home after superannuation without obtaining a civilian licence is in unlicensed possession of a firearm.

definitions.plain_english: Good faith means acting honestly and sincerely, believing that what you are doing is permitted or required by the Arms Act, even if you later turn out to be mistaken. definitions.definition: An identification mark, in relation to a firearm or ammunition, means any name, number or other mark stamped or otherwise shown on a firearm or ammunition in a manner approved by the Central Government, including the name of the maker and the manufacturer's number, which serves to identify the origin and authenticity of the weapon or ammunition.
definitions.plain_english: An identification mark is any name, serial number, or other marking that a manufacturer places on a gun or ammunition to show who made it and to uniquely identify that particular weapon. Think of it like a vehicle's chassis number or a product's serial number — it links the firearm back to its maker and allows authorities to track it. The government decides the approved format and placement of these marks.
real_world_examples: A licensed firearms manufacturer in Jabalpur stamps each pistol with its factory name and a unique serial number on the barrel and frame before selling it to a licensed dealer — these constitute the identification marks required under Section 8.

During a police raid in Mumbai, officers recover a country-made revolver with its serial number filed off. Since the identification mark has been obliterated, the possessor is presumed under Section 8(3) to have tampered with it and faces criminal prosecution.

An arms dealer in Delhi is found selling a foreign-imported rifle that bears no manufacturer's name or number. Because the firearm lacks a Central Government-approved identification mark, the sale is prohibited under Section 8(2) and the dealer is liable for punishment under Section 25.

A gun smuggler in Punjab alters the engraved manufacturer's number on a semi-automatic rifle using a grinding tool to prevent tracing by law enforcement. This act of altering the identification mark is an offence under Section 8(1) of the Arms Act.

The Ordnance Factory Board in Kanpur stamps each service rifle issued to paramilitary forces with a government-approved alphanumeric code and factory emblem — this constitutes the official identification mark enabling unit-level tracking and accountability.

A licensed arms dealer in Hyderabad acquires a second-hand shotgun from a private seller but notices the manufacturer's number is partially scratched. Before completing the transfer, the dealer reports this to the licensing authority to avoid liability under Section 8.
what_it_covers: The manufacturer's name stamped or engraved on the body of a firearm in a manner approved by the Central Government.
The manufacturer's unique serial or production number marked on a firearm or ammunition, enabling individual identification of each unit.
Any other symbol, code, or alphanumeric marking officially placed on a firearm or ammunition by a licensed manufacturer to denote origin, batch, or model as per government-approved standards.
Government proof marks or inspection stamps placed on firearms after testing at authorised proof houses, where such marks are required to appear on the weapon.
what_it_excludes: Informal scratches, paint markings, or owner-applied engravings that are not stamped or shown in a manner approved by the Central Government.
Markings placed on firearm accessories, holsters, cases, or cleaning kits that are not part of the firearm or ammunition itself.
Internal component part numbers that are not externally stamped or shown on the firearm in a manner visible and approved under government specifications.
Labels or stickers affixed by dealers or retailers for inventory purposes, which are not official manufacturer or government-approved identification marks.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a firearm bears a valid identification mark determines whether its sale or transfer is lawful under Section 8(2); absence of such a mark triggers a statutory presumption under Section 8(3) that the possessor has tampered with it, exposing them to prosecution and punishment of two to five years imprisonment under Section 25(1B). Obliterating, removing, altering, or forging an identification mark under Section 8(1) is independently punishable and directly enables offences related to illicit trafficking and tracing of weapons.

definitions.definition: "Illicit trafficking" means the acquisition, sale, delivery, movement or transfer of arms or ammunition from or across the territory of one country to that of another, in contravention of the laws of the countries concerned, including clandestine or deceptive procurement, storage, or movement of firearms and ammunition outside authorised and licensed channels, as used in the context of Section 25 of the Arms Act.
definitions.plain_english: Illicit trafficking refers to the illegal buying, selling, moving, or transferring of guns and ammunition across borders or within a country without proper government permission or licences. It covers all hidden or deceptive dealings in weapons that bypass the official legal system. This includes smuggling firearms into or out of India, or secretly supplying weapons to criminal groups without any authorisation.
real_world_examples: A consignment of unlicensed pistols and cartridges is smuggled from Pakistan into Punjab through unofficial border crossings and distributed to criminal gangs — this constitutes illicit trafficking as the arms move across international borders outside authorised channels.

A dealer in Maharashtra secretly sells a large cache of prohibited AK-47 rifles to an organised crime syndicate operating in Mumbai, without any licence or government approval, representing domestic illicit trafficking of prohibited arms.

Arms recovered from Naxalite groups in Chhattisgarh are traced back to a supply chain that smuggled them from Nepal through Bihar, involving multiple illegal transfers across state and international boundaries — a classic illicit trafficking network.

A person in Tamil Nadu converts legally registered sporting rifles into automatic weapons and sells them clandestinely to terrorists operating in Jammu & Kashmir, routing them through multiple states without any transfer authorisation — constituting illicit trafficking through illegal conversion and unlawful transfer.

Counterfeit and unregistered country-made firearms manufactured in Munger, Bihar are transported and sold to criminal networks in Delhi and Uttar Pradesh through unlicensed intermediaries, representing organised illicit trafficking within India.
what_it_covers: Smuggling of firearms or ammunition across Indian international borders without import or export authorisation under Section 11 of the Arms Act.
Clandestine sale, transfer, or movement of prohibited arms or prohibited ammunition to criminal groups or individuals without a licence, in contravention of Section 7.

Illegal procurement and supply of arms through unlicensed dealers or intermediaries, including conversion of legal firearms into prohibited categories and their subsequent distribution outside authorised channels.
Movement of arms or ammunition across state boundaries through organised crime syndicates or terror networks, where no lawful authorisation or licence exists at any stage of the supply chain.
Covert importation or exportation of arms disguised as civilian goods or routed through unofficial border crossings to evade customs and licensing authorities.
what_it_excludes: Lawful import or export of arms and ammunition by authorised government agencies, armed forces of the Union, or licensed dealers acting in compliance with Section 10 and Section 11 of the Arms Act.
Licensed transfer or transport of firearms and ammunition between licensed dealers or between a dealer and a licence-holder, conducted within the framework of the Arms Act and Arms Rules 2016.
Possession or carriage of arms by an individual holding a valid licence under Section 3, even if the arms are moved across state lines, provided all conditions of the licence are complied with.
Surrender or deposit of arms to the district magistrate or police authority as mandated under Section 21, which is a lawful and authorised movement of arms.
Seizure, confiscation, or transport of arms by police officers or armed forces personnel acting in official capacity under lawful arrest or enforcement operations.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as illicit trafficking directly determines the severity of punishment under Section 25, which prescribes a minimum of seven years imprisonment extendable to life imprisonment for contraventions involving bringing arms into or out of India under Section 11, and up to life imprisonment for dealings in prohibited arms under Section 7. Establishing illicit trafficking is critical to prosecuting organised arms smuggling networks and triggers provisions relating to organised crime, tracing of weapons, and forfeiture of seized arms.

definitions.definition: In section 6 of the Arms Act, the expression 'imitation firearm' means anything which has the appearance of being a firearm, whether it is capable of discharging any shot, bullet or other missile or not.
definitions.plain_english: An imitation firearm is any object that looks like a real gun, regardless of whether it can actually fire bullets or any projectile. It does not have to work like a real firearm — its appearance alone is sufficient to bring it within this definition. The law treats such objects with caution because they can be converted into functional weapons.
real_world_examples: A realistic-looking plastic toy pistol sold at a market in Delhi that visually resembles a semi-automatic handgun but cannot fire any projectile qualifies as an imitation firearm under Section 6.

A deactivated or 'decommissioned' revolver purchased from a prop shop in Mumbai that has been rendered non-functional but retains the full external appearance of a working firearm is covered by this definition.
A metal replica of a World War II-era rifle used as a decorative piece or wall-mount in a Kolkata residence, which cannot discharge ammunition, would constitute an imitation firearm.

A stage or film prop gun used on a Bollywood set in Mumbai that is designed to look exactly like a real pistol — even if fitted only with blank-firing capability or no mechanism at all — falls within the definition of an imitation firearm.

A 3D-printed shell of a handgun, having the full outward appearance of a firearm but containing no firing mechanism, manufactured or possessed in Bengaluru, would be treated as an imitation firearm for the purposes of Section 6.
what_it_covers: Any object — regardless of material (plastic, metal, resin) — that visually resembles a firearm, even if entirely incapable of firing a shot, bullet or missile.
Realistic replica or dummy guns used in film, theatre or as decorative collectibles that have the outward appearance of a real weapon.
Deactivated or decommissioned real firearms whose internal mechanisms have been rendered non-functional but which retain the external appearance of a working firearm.
3D-printed or handcrafted shells or casings shaped to look like pistols, rifles or revolvers, irrespective of the absence of any firing mechanism.
Blank-firing replica pistols or starter guns that visually mimic real firearms, even if their barrels are obstructed or modified to prevent live ammunition discharge.
what_it_excludes: Objects that do not bear any visual resemblance to a firearm, such as abstract or clearly cartoonish toy guns that no reasonable person would mistake for a real weapon.
Actual functional firearms that are capable of discharging shot, bullet or other missile — these fall under the definition of 'firearm' and are governed by separate provisions of the Act.
Water pistols, foam dart guns or other clearly non-realistic children's toys whose shape and form do not replicate the appearance of a real firearm.
Component parts of a firearm (such as a barrel, stock or trigger guard sold separately) that do not by themselves present the complete visual appearance of a firearm.
Diagrams, drawings, photographs or two-dimensional representations of firearms, as these are not physical objects having the appearance of being a firearm.

definitions.definition: The expression 'lawful arrest' is not formally defined in the Arms Act, but as used in Section 28, it refers to an arrest or detention carried out by a competent authority — such as a police officer or other authorised public servant — in accordance with the procedures and powers established by law, including the Code of Criminal Procedure, and any other applicable statute conferring such power.
definitions.plain_english: A 'lawful arrest' means an arrest that is made by a person who has the legal authority to do so, following the correct legal procedures. definitions.definition: The term 'moral turpitude' is not formally defined in the Arms Act, but as used in Section 9(1)(a)(ii), it refers to conduct that is inherently base, vile, or depraved, contrary to accepted moral standards and duties owed by persons to one another or to society, such that a conviction for an offence involving such conduct disqualifies a person from acquiring, possessing, or carrying firearms or ammunition for a period of five years after expiration of the sentence of imprisonment.
definitions.plain_english: Moral turpitude refers to behaviour that is considered seriously wrong or shameful by society's basic moral standards — actions that show a person is dishonest, cruel, or deeply unethical. If someone is convicted of a crime that involves this kind of conduct and is sent to prison, they are barred from owning or carrying a gun for five years after their release. It is not just any crime, but one that reflects badly on a person's character and trustworthiness.
real_world_examples: A person convicted of rape under Section 376 IPC and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment is released; they cannot apply for or possess a firearms licence for five years after completing the sentence, as rape is an offence involving both violence and moral turpitude.

A money-lender in a rural district is convicted of cheating (Section 420 IPC) through systematic fraud involving fabricated land documents and sentenced to two years' imprisonment; upon release, he is prohibited from acquiring any firearm or ammunition for five years as cheating is widely held to involve moral turpitude.

A government clerk convicted of accepting bribes (Prevention of Corruption Act) and sentenced to imprisonment is barred from possessing his licensed revolver during the five-year disqualification period following release, since corruption offences are recognised as involving moral turpitude.

A person convicted of kidnapping for ransom under Section 364A IPC and sentenced to imprisonment is denied a fresh arms licence application within five years of release, as kidnapping for ransom is an offence involving violence and moral turpitude under established judicial interpretation.

A landlord convicted of human trafficking under the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act and sentenced to prison is disqualified from possessing firearms for five years post-sentence, as trafficking is a classic example of an offence involving moral turpitude.

A person convicted of dacoity (Section 395 IPC) involving violence and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment is prohibited from carrying even a licensed firearm during the five-year post-release disqualification period under Section 9 of the Arms Act.

definitions.plain_english: A muzzle loading gun is an old-fashioned type of gun where you load the gunpowder and bullet from the front end (the barrel opening) rather than from the back like modern firearms. A village community watchman in Chhattisgarh is found in possession of an unlicensed muzzle loading gun; because even muzzle loading guns require a licence under Section 3, he faces prosecution under the Arms Act.

definitions.definition: Arms of such description as may be specified by the Central Government in a notification issued under Section 24A or Section 24B in the Official Gazette, in relation to a disturbed area where extensive disturbance of public peace and tranquillity exists or is imminently apprehended, and in respect of which special restrictions on possession or carrying are imposed for the prevention of offences involving the use of arms. definitions.plain_english: Notified arms are specific types of weapons that the Central Government officially lists in a government notice when an area is facing serious law and order problems or riots. Once the government publishes this notice, ordinary people in that area are not allowed to keep or carry those weapons, even if they had a valid licence. The government essentially puts those particular weapons on a temporary ban list for a troubled region to prevent violence.
real_world_examples: During prolonged communal riots in a district of Uttar Pradesh, the Central Government issues a gazette notification specifying that all licensed revolvers and pistols held by civilians within the specified district limits are 'notified arms' and must be deposited at the nearest police station before the fourth day after publication.

In a northeastern state affected by insurgency, the Central Government notifies that all semi-automatic rifles and shotguns held by civilians in a specified area are notified arms, prohibiting their possession during a 90-day period and authorising army officers to search vehicles and premises for such weapons.

During violent agitations in a border district of Manipur, the Central Government issues a Section 24B notification specifying country-made pistols and single-barrel guns as notified arms, prohibiting any person from carrying them through public places such as markets, roads, or railway stations in the area.

In the aftermath of large-scale political violence in a West Bengal district, the Central Government notifies licensed firearms including muzzle-loading guns and smooth bore guns as notified arms under Section 24A, requiring all holders to deposit them and deeming further possession unlawful from the date of gazette publication.

Following terrorist incidents in a Jammu region district, the Central Government specifies high-calibre rifles and certain categories of ammunition as notified arms under both Sections 24A and 24B, empowering designated officers to seize any such arms found on persons or in vehicles passing through the area.
what_it_covers: Any firearm of a description expressly specified in a Central Government gazette notification issued under Section 24A or 24B in relation to a disturbed area, including licensed firearms that would otherwise be lawfully held.

Ammunition associated with the specified arms, as Section 24A(4)(a) expressly provides that for purposes of that section 'arms' includes ammunition, thereby making notified ammunition subject to the same deposit and prohibition obligations.

Arms carried by or in the possession of any person — whether on their body, in a vehicle, vessel, animal-borne container, or in premises — within the limits of the specified disturbed area during the notified period.

Arms that are secreted or concealed on a person, in premises, or in any conveyance or receptacle within the notified area, which authorised officers are empowered to search for and seize under the notification.
what_it_excludes: Arms not falling within the description specified in the particular gazette notification — any weapon type not explicitly listed in the notification remains outside the scope of 'notified arms' and is unaffected by the Section 24A or 24B prohibition.

definitions.plain_english: An 'offence' under the Arms Act refers to any act that breaks the rules set out in the Act — for example, possessing a gun without a licence, selling weapons illegally, or carrying prohibited arms. If a person does something the Arms Act says they must not do, or fails to do something the Act requires them to do, they have committed an offence. Such offences can lead to arrest, prosecution, and imprisonment or fines.
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai is found in possession of a country-made pistol without any licence issued under the Arms Act — this constitutes an offence under Section 25 read with the definition of offence applicable in Section 33.

A licensed arms dealer in Delhi sells a firearm to a person who has been convicted of a violent crime within the last five years, violating Section 9 of the Arms Act, thereby committing an offence punishable under Section 33.

An individual in Uttar Pradesh is caught transporting prohibited arms such as an automatic rifle across state lines without lawful authority — this constitutes a cognizable offence under the Arms Act.

A resident of Chennai who holds a valid arms licence uses it to carry a firearm into a prohibited zone near a polling station during elections, violating licence conditions and thereby committing an offence under the Act.

A gun repair shop owner in Hyderabad repairs a firearm for a customer without the customer producing a valid licence, knowingly facilitating an unlicensed possession — both parties may be liable for an offence under the Act.
A person who fires a gun in a public place in celebration (celebratory gunfire) in Rajasthan without lawful authority commits an offence under the Arms Act as amended.
what_it_covers: Possessing or carrying firearms or ammunition without a valid licence issued under the Arms Act.
Manufacturing, selling, repairing, or transferring arms or ammunition in contravention of the Act or without requisite authorisation.
Carrying or using prohibited arms or prohibited ammunition by any person not lawfully authorised to do so.
Violation of any condition attached to a licence, such as carrying a firearm outside the permitted area or for an unlawful purpose.
Selling or transferring a firearm or ammunition to a person convicted of a violent offence or of unsound mind, in breach of Section 9.
what_it_excludes: Lawful possession, use, or transfer of arms and ammunition by persons holding a valid licence and acting strictly within its conditions.
Acts by armed forces of the Union or other exempted government agencies operating under lawful authority, which do not constitute offences under this Act.
Possession or use of articles specifically excluded from the definition of 'arms', such as ordinary walking sticks, lathis, or toys incapable of conversion into serviceable weapons.
Minor procedural or administrative non-compliance that does not rise to a level of criminal culpability as envisaged under the penal provisions of the Act.
Acts performed in good faith under a bona fide belief of lawful authority, where the Act or courts recognise a valid defence.
